newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain to work at easing HK handover tensions.
newsitem.headline: Britain to work at easing HK handover tensions.

text.p: Britain's minister overseeing Hong Kong's 1997 return to Chinese rule said on Monday that London would strive to persuade Beijing to allow the territory's elected legislature to exist beyond the handover.

But Jeremy Hanley, Minister of State at the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, dodged questions on what action Britain would take if China did abolish the present chamber and replace it with a provisional body.
"We will continue to try to persuade the Chinese that we think it is a thoroughly bad idea," Hanley told reporters as he stopped off in Hong Kong at the end of an Asian tour.
China has vowed to dismantle the present fully elected legislature in retaliation for a string of democratic reforms implemented unilaterally by colonial governor Chris Patten.

Hanley, who met members of the British colony's Executive Council, or cabinet, on Monday said that China's decision to set up a provisional chamber would be raised in talks between Britain's Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkin and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 26.

Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, 1997. In the run-up to the handover, Hong Kong's six million people face uncertainty over the question of rights and freedoms after 1997.

Hanley, whose meeting with senior Chinese official Lu Ping in Beijing earlier this month was widely perceived to have helped further smooth Sino-British relations, also hinted that the two governments may have finally reached a deal to cooperate on formal ceremonies to mark the handover.
